sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Multiple Pacific storms will impact western Washington this week and weekend for gusty winds, lowland rain and high elevation mountain snow. Large swells will reach the coast on Friday.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Wednesday night)
paragraphs: Our next Pacific frontal system is upon us with rain spreading inland this afternoon. The air mass is slightly unstable with a chance of thunderstorms across SW WA (mainly this afternoon and evening). Expect windy conditions along the coast and North interior with south winds gusting to 30-35 MPH.

Another deep low spins over the NE Pacific on Tuesday and Wednesday for another round of gusty winds, lowland rain and high elevation snow. Winds will be strongest along the coast and North Interior with south/southeast wind gusts to 40-50 MPH - Wind Advisories are in effect. Winds will stay gusty through Wednesday afternoon then ease Wednesday night. In addition, minor coastal flooding is possible around the time of high tide Wednesday morning for the San Juans and western Whatcom county. 33

sections.title: Long term (Thursday through Monday)
paragraphs: A trio of strong Pacific systems are poised to impact Western WA Friday through Sunday. The main impact will again be strong winds, especially over the coast where gusts may exceed 50 MPH. We may also see gusty winds to 30-40 MPH in the interior as well. These systems will also generate large swells that will reach the WA coast Friday with seas over 20 ft possible. Rainfall will be heavy at times along the coast and over the Olympics. This may bring the Skokomish River close to minor flood stage. We are also closely monitoring the storm tide predictions as well as a few locations may see minor coastal flooding on Saturday. The last system moves in on Sunday - more wind and rain - with the weather easing moving into Sunday night and Monday. 33

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A frontal system will continue to move across the terminals, with widespread rain bringing ceilings. Reduced visibilities have been observed with heavier pockets of rain down to to 3-5 mi. Overnight the ceilings are expected to lift up to low-end VFR, with an additional front passing through late Tuesday with more rain and lowering ceilings/visibilities back down to MVFR. Winds will generally remain out of the southeast or southwest, with the strongest winds through Tuesday morning, and again Tuesday evening. Gusts up to 20-30 kt with higher gusts to 35 kt along the coast.

KSEA...VFR conditions likely rebound this evening, but again lower into MVFR with the next round of rain which will arrive around 15z Tuesday morning. Southerly surface winds easing tonight, but increasing again Tuesday afternoon and evening with gusts again to 25 kt.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A series of frontal systems will impact the waters through the week. Widespread rain will pass over the waters at times, with rates potentially becoming heavy enough to drop visibilities significantly for mariners. There is a 20% chance of thunder for portions of the coastal waters with the front moving through this evening, and again Tuesday afternoon into Wednesday.

Widespread gusty southerly winds will continue for much of the week across the majority of the waters. Winds with the front moving through Monday afternoon will remain in the 20 to 30 kt range for the coastal waters and west Strait of Juan de Fuca, and Puget Sound through the Northern Inland Waters (including the east Strait of Juan de Fuca and Admiralty Inlet). A stronger system on Tuesday into Wednesday will produce widespread and frequent gale force gusts for the coastal waters and east strait. Wind gusts will likely remain above 20 kt through Friday with another stronger system producing additional gale gusts for the coastal waters and east Strait of Juan de Fuca, with a similar system on Saturday into Sunday. Models have winds finally decreasing below 20 kt early next week.

Seas: 10-12 ft tonight through Tuesday, increasing to 17 to 19 ft late Tuesday into Thursday before decreasing to 10 to 14 ft Thursday. Models have a significant push up to 20 to 23 ft Friday into the weekend with seas decreasing on Monday back down to 10 to 14 ft.
HPR

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: After a storm system clips the area Tuesday, expect drier weather Wednesday and Thursday before another storm system brings widespread rain and breezy conditions to the area Friday into the weekend. Sneaker waves will be a threat through the week with another round of high surf conditions appearing increasingly likely Saturday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Sunday...Radar imagery and surface observations as of early Monday afternoon depicts a band of widespread rain moving through northwest Oregon and southwest Washington as a frontal system enters the region. We're also experiencing some breezy southerly winds with gusts up to 30-35 mph along the coast and up to 20 mph along the I-5 corridor. Behind the front, satellite imagery reveals scattered/broken cloud cover. A relatively warmer surface with colder air aloft is resulting in increased atmospheric instability, with SPC mesoanalysis showing MUCAPE values of 100-250 J/kg across the offshore waters, central Oregon coast, and southern Willamette Valley. This instability will gradually spread northward over the next few hours as the front progresses northeastward. As a result, there is a 10-20% chance for thunderstorms across the region through 7 PM this evening. Any passing thunderstorms may produce lightning, heavy rain, erratic winds, and/or small hail.

On Tuesday, another upper-level shortwave trough will move into the Pacific Northwest, swinging another front into the area while upper-level ridging begins to amplify east of the Cascades. This ridging will act to limit rain to the coast, Coast Range, and inland areas north of US-20 Tuesday morning, then steadily displace rain chances further north into Washington through the afternoon. A rather sharp gradient in rainfall totals on Tuesday is expected from south to north, with little to no rain south of US-20, less than 0.2 inch for the interior lowlands south of Longview and the coast south of Tillamook, 0.25-0.5 inches for the SW WA Cascades and Tillamook to the state line, and 0.5-1 inch for Pacific County. Heavier rain associated with this atmospheric river is expected over the Olympic Peninsula. Expect another round of breezy southerly winds with gusts as high as 30-40 mph along the coast north of Tillamook and SW WA west of I-5 through Tuesday evening.

Upper-level ridging will reach its peak amplitude on Wednesday, supporting dry and unseasonably warm temperatures across interior valleys with high temperatures forecast in the low to mid 60s. Daily record high temperatures look to remain out of reach for most locations, though the record values of 64F at Portland (PDX) and Hillsboro (HIO) set in 1989 and 66F at Vancouver (VUO) set in 1904, 1907, and 1930 may be in jeopardy. Thursday is expected to be a transition day as upper ridging begins shifting east as upper troughing begins pushing into the northeastern Pacific. Daytime temperatures will lower a few degrees, though will still be unseasonably warm in the low 60s across interior valleys. Mostly dry weather is expected through the day except for a 20-40% chance of showers along the coast, mainly due to uncertainty on specific timing of the rain from the approaching trough.

There is high confidence that an upper-level low pressure system will become situated over the northeast Pacific west of Canada from late Thursday/Friday into the weekend, returning troughing to the Pacific Northwest. Multiple surface frontal systems are expected to move through the region during this time, bringing repeated chances for widespread rain and breezy winds. There is still uncertainty with specific rainfall amounts and peak wind gusts; however, we can say for certain that it will be wet. This is shaping up to be another atmospheric river event as long- range ensembles indicate a 60-70% chance for vapor transport to exceed 500 kg/(ms) at the leading edge of this trough on Friday somewhere along the Oregon coast with higher probabilities of vapor transport values remaining above 250 kg/(ms) through Saturday. Chances for rain amounts exceeding 2 inches from Friday morning through Sunday morning are 20-30% along the I-5 corridor and 60-80% for the coast and Coast Range. Additionally, the coast and Coast Range have a 20-40% chance of total rain amounts exceeding 3 inches of rain for the same time period. Increasingly saturated soils from multiple weather systems could allow for greater runoff into area rivers, meaning at least isolated flooding cannot be ruled out. People should also clear gutters and storm drains of any leaves or debris to prevent urban flooding. Across the Cascades, it appears that this system would be warm enough to keep snow levels between 5500-6500 feet, keeping the passes snow-free.

When it comes to winds, there is a 20-40% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 60 mph along the coast Friday and Saturday, with the highest chances on Friday. Wind gusts of this magnitude could result in scattered or widespread power outages or tree damage. Along the I-5 corridor, there is a 20-40% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 40 mph, which could result in isolated power outages or tree damage. To prepare, make sure to secure loose outdoor items.            -10/03

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 06Z Wednesday...A front has moved well east of the Cascades this evening. In its wake, scattered showers continue to affect mainly the Cascades where mountain obscurations persist. Coastal and Willamette Valley taf sites are generally VFR. However, some lower ceilings and visibility restrictions are underway as the lower atmosphere stabilizes and winds weaken. High clouds can already be seen approaching the Oregon coast from the West so there will be a window over the next several hours where fog will try and develop at sites, particularly KHIO and KAST. Cannot rule it out elsewhere, but winds elsewhere will make lower IFR ceilings more likely than true ground fog. A warm front will clip the northwestern half of the forecast area Tuesday morning. This will bring additional light rain and another round of more persistent MVFR conditions. Winds will increase as it lifts past the region, particularly along the coast after 15-18z Tuesday. As the warm front lifts north of the region, most taf sites should trend VFR between 18z Tuesday and 06z Wednesday.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...While conditions are VFR at the moment, it does appear there is an increasing risk for MVFR conditions to develop overnight as the lower atmosphere stabilizes. As a warm front brings lifts northeastward and clips the region, probabilities for MVFR conditions at any given hour rise to 50% in the 12-18z Tuesday time period. Until then, it appears there should be enough low cloud cover and/or wind that the the probability that fog develops is less than 20%. Current southerly winds should switch back to easterly over the next few hours.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Small craft conditions across the water tonight in the wake of a front. Winds will increase Tuesday and Wednesday as a front moves across the waters. There is a 50-90% chance for gales north of Cape Falcon where a Gale Warning has been issued. The winds south of Cape Falcon will either be low-end gales or high- end small craft and have issued a Gale Watch. Marginal gales continue Wednesday as a cold front moves into the waters. A building west swell will result in 14-18 ft seas at around 14 seconds.
A stronger frontal system will increase winds and seas on Friday. with a 10-20% chance for Storm force winds on Friday and a 60-80% chance of 20+ ft seas on Saturday.       -11

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 10-12 ft at 13-15 seconds increases to 14-16 ft midweek. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.

There is also the potential for tidal overflow flooding Wednesday and Thursday as the tide plus anomaly are forecasted between 10 and 11 ft (MLLW). This could lead to further water inundation and coastal erosion.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 20-24 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast on Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave.      -11
